title: Data Types and Records
overview: Topic 10.1 is about choosing how each item of data is stored. At AS level the pseudocode types are INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN and DATE, plus ARRAY and FILE for collections and stored files. Exam questions ask for the type of each variable in an identifier table, with a reason tied to what the value is and how it will be used. The second half covers the record: a user-defined type that keeps several fields of different types together under one identifier. You need to be able to write the TYPE … ENDTYPE definition, declare a variable or an array of that type, and put data into fields and read it back out with dot notation.
syllabusPoints: Select and use appropriate data types for a problem solution, including integer, real, char, string, Boolean and date (pseudocode data types INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE, ARRAY, FILE).
Show understanding of the purpose of a record structure to hold a set of data of different data types under one identifier.
Write pseudocode to define a record structure.
Write pseudocode to read data from a record structure and save data to a record structure.

definitions.definition: The kind of value an identifier can hold. It fixes which values are allowed, how much memory is set aside and which operations make sense, such as arithmetic on numbers or joining on strings.
A type built into the language that holds a single value and cannot be split into smaller parts, such as INTEGER, REAL, CHAR or BOOLEAN.
A signed whole number with no fractional part, for example -3, 0 or 250.
A signed number that can have a fractional part; in pseudocode a REAL literal is written with a decimal point and a digit on each side, for example 4.0 or -0.75.
Exactly one character, written in single quotes, for example 'Y' or '7'.
A sequence of zero or more characters, written in double quotes; "" is the empty string.
A type with only two values, TRUE and FALSE, used for flags and the results of conditions.
A calendar date (day, month and year), written in pseudocode as dd/mm/yyyy, which the language can compare and calculate with.
A type the programmer defines that groups a fixed set of named fields, possibly of different data types, so that all the data about one item is held under one identifier.
One named, typed part of a record, reached with dot notation such as Student.Name.

sections.title: Primitive data types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR and BOOLEAN
content: When you plan an algorithm, each identifier in the identifier table needs a data type as well as a name and a purpose. The simplest types are the primitive (also called atomic) types, which the language provides directly and which each hold one indivisible value.

INTEGER holds signed whole numbers, so it suits anything that is counted rather than measured: loop counters, array indexes, the number of items in stock, a year. REAL holds numbers that may have a fractional part, so it suits measurements and results of division, such as a height in metres, a price or an average. CHAR holds exactly one character, for instance a menu choice 'A' to 'D' or a grade. BOOLEAN holds TRUE or FALSE and is the natural type for any yes/no fact or flag, such as whether a value has been found.

Cambridge pseudocode also fixes how literal values of each type are written. An INTEGER literal is plain digits, optionally with a minus sign. A REAL literal always has a decimal point with at least one digit on each side, so 5.0 not 5. or .5. A CHAR literal goes in single quotes and a STRING literal in double quotes. TRUE and FALSE are written in capitals without quotes.
bullets: Counted values (how many, which position) are INTEGER; measured or calculated values that may not be whole are REAL.
Any value produced by '/' division should be stored as REAL, even when the inputs are integers.
CHAR is for one character only; 'Y' is a CHAR but "Yes" must be a STRING.
Use BOOLEAN for two-state data rather than an INTEGER 0/1 or a STRING "yes"/"no"; it can be tested directly in a condition.

examples.label: Declaring primitive variables and assigning literals
examples.content:
DECLARE ItemsInBasket : INTEGER
DECLARE MeanSpeed : REAL
DECLARE MenuChoice : CHAR
DECLARE IsMember : BOOLEAN

ItemsInBasket ← 12
MeanSpeed ← 48.5          // REAL: decimal point with digits both sides
MenuChoice ← 'C'          // CHAR: single quotes, one character
IsMember ← FALSE          // BOOLEAN: no quotes

sections.title: STRING, DATE, ARRAY and FILE
content: A STRING is a sequence of characters, so it is a structured rather than atomic type: you can take its length or pick out part of it. It may hold no characters at all (the empty string ""), which is useful as a starting value when a string is built up in a loop. The number 12 and the string "12" are different values: 12 can be used in arithmetic, while "12" is two characters and "12" & "3" gives "123".

A DATE holds a day, month and year. It exists as a separate type because programs often need to compare dates or work out the gap between them, and a date held as text cannot do this reliably: compared as strings, "09/05/2025" counts as earlier than "10/01/2024" because the first characters, '0' and '1', settle the comparison, even though the 2025 date is really the later one. In pseudocode a date literal is written dd/mm/yyyy, for example 21/06/2008.

The syllabus list also contains ARRAY and FILE. ARRAY is used when many values of the same type are kept under one identifier, for example DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER (see 10.2). FILE is the type of data stored outside the program, for example a text file opened with OPENFILE and read line by line (see 10.3). In an identifier table these appear in the data type column just like the primitive types.
bullets: STRING is for text and for codes that are never used in arithmetic, even if they contain only digits.
The empty string "" is a valid STRING value with length 0.
DATE lets dates be compared and subtracted correctly; STRING dates only compare character by character.
ARRAY and FILE are also pseudocode data types: an identifier table may show ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER or FILE as the type.

examples.label: STRING and DATE in pseudocode
examples.content:
DECLARE FullName : STRING
DECLARE Initials : STRING
DECLARE JoinDate : DATE
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER

FullName ← "Leila Haddad"
Initials ← ""                // empty string, filled in later
JoinDate ← 04/09/2025        // DATE literal dd/mm/yyyy
Initials ← Initials & 'L' & 'H'
OUTPUT Initials                 // LH

sections.title: Selecting and justifying a data type
content: In Paper 2 you are often given a scenario and asked to complete an identifier table or to state and justify the data type of a variable. The type should follow from two questions: what values can this item take, and what will the program do with it? A justification earns the mark when it names the property that decides the choice, for instance 'always a whole number', 'may contain a fractional part', 'only ever one of two values' or 'contains a leading zero and is not used in calculations'.

The commonest trap is data that looks numeric but is really an identifier: telephone numbers, ISBNs, postcodes, product codes and candidate numbers. These are STRING because they may start with 0 or contain spaces, letters or '+', and nobody adds or averages them. On the other side, choose REAL, not INTEGER, whenever the value could legitimately be non-whole, and INTEGER, not REAL, for anything used as a counter or an array index.
bullets: State the type, then give a reason based on the data (whole number, fractional part, one character, two states, calendar date, text).
Numeric-looking codes that are never used in arithmetic are STRING, which also keeps leading zeros.
Money is usually REAL (for example 14.99); a quantity or count is INTEGER.
A single-letter code such as a size 'S', 'M', 'L' is CHAR; a value that is sometimes more than one character is STRING.

examples.label: Identifier table for a gym membership program
examples.content:
Identifier     | Data type | Justification
MemberCode     | STRING    | e.g. "0041-B": leading zero and a letter, never used in arithmetic
Surname        | STRING    | text of varying length
DateJoined     | DATE      | a calendar date that is compared with today's date
VisitsThisYear | INTEGER   | a count, always a whole number
MonthlyFee     | REAL      | money, e.g. 27.50, has a fractional part
AgeBand        | CHAR      | one letter: 'J' junior, 'A' adult, 'S' senior
IsActive       | BOOLEAN   | only two possible states, active or not
Phone          | STRING    | starts with 0 or +, may contain spaces

sections.title: The purpose of a record structure
content: Some data items belong together because they all describe one thing. A library book has a title (STRING), an ISBN (STRING), a year of publication (INTEGER), a price (REAL) and a flag for whether it is on loan (BOOLEAN). These values have different types, so they cannot share an array, which needs every element to be the same type.

A record solves this. The programmer defines a new record type that lists the fields and their types; the language does not supply it, which is why a record is called a user-defined type, and because it is built from other types it is also called a composite type. A variable of that type then holds one complete set of field values under a single identifier, so everything about one book travels together: it can be assigned, passed to a procedure or stored in an array as one unit.

Be careful not to confuse this with a record in a database table (topic 8). A record data structure is a type inside a program; a database record is a row in a table. The idea is similar, one set of values about one entity, but the exam context tells you which is meant.
bullets: Purpose: to hold a set of related data of different data types under one identifier.
Each field has its own name and its own data type; the set of fields is fixed when the type is defined.
A record is user-defined (the programmer declares it) and composite (made of other types).
An array holds many values of one type; a record holds several named values of possibly different types.

sections.title: Defining a record type and declaring record variables
content: A record type is defined with TYPE, the type name, one DECLARE line per field, and ENDTYPE. The definition only describes the layout: no data exists yet, in the same way that the word INTEGER on its own stores nothing. A separate DECLARE statement then creates a variable of the new type, and every such variable gets its own copy of every field.

Choose each field's type using the same rules as for ordinary variables (see the section on justifying a data type), and give the type a name that makes clear it is a type, such as StudentRecord or BookType, so it is not mistaken for a variable.
bullets: TYPE … ENDTYPE defines the structure; DECLARE Variable : TypeName creates storage.
Every field line inside the TYPE block has the form DECLARE FieldName : DataType.
Two variables of the same record type have independent fields: changing Student1.Name leaves Student2.Name alone.
A field can itself be an ARRAY or another record type, but at AS level fields are usually primitive types, STRING or DATE.

examples.label: Defining StudentRecord and declaring variables
examples.content:
TYPE StudentRecord
   DECLARE StudentID : STRING
   DECLARE Name : STRING
   DECLARE DateOfBirth : DATE
   DECLARE TestMark : INTEGER
   DECLARE FeesPaid : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE

DECLARE Student : StudentRecord
DECLARE Prefect : StudentRecord

sections.title: Saving data to and reading data from a record
content: Each field is reached with dot notation: the variable identifier, a full stop, then the field identifier, as in Student.TestMark. A field used this way behaves exactly like an ordinary variable of the field's type. To save data to a record you assign to its fields, either from literals, from calculations or directly from INPUT. To read data from a record you use the fields in expressions, conditions or OUTPUT statements.

You cannot assign a single value to the whole record variable (Student ← "Aisha" is wrong, because Student is not a STRING). The one whole-record operation allowed is copying one record variable into another of the same type, for example Prefect ← Student, which copies every field at once.
bullets: Write: Student.Name ← "Aisha" or INPUT Student.Name.
Read: OUTPUT Student.Name or IF Student.FeesPaid = FALSE THEN …
A field has the type given in the TYPE block, so Student.TestMark + 5 is INTEGER arithmetic.
Record ← Record of the same type copies all fields; Record ← single value is an error.

examples.label: Saving to and reading from one record
examples.content:
// save data to the record
Student.StudentID ← "S1042"
Student.Name ← "Aisha"
Student.DateOfBirth ← 14/03/2008
INPUT Student.TestMark                // user types 72
Student.FeesPaid ← FALSE

// read data from the record
IF Student.FeesPaid = FALSE
   THEN
      OUTPUT Student.Name, " has fees outstanding"
ENDIF
Student.TestMark ← Student.TestMark + 3   // moderation adds 3 marks
OUTPUT Student.Name, ": ", Student.TestMark

Output:
Aisha has fees outstanding
Aisha: 75

Only TestMark changes (72 to 75); StudentID, DateOfBirth and FeesPaid keep the values saved at the start.

sections.title: Arrays of records
content: One record variable holds one item. To hold a whole class or a whole stock list, declare an array whose element type is the record type. Each element is then a complete record, and a field of one element is written with the index first and the field second: Class[3].Name is the Name field of the third student.

Because the element number can be a loop counter, the same few lines can save data into, or read data out of, every record in turn. This is the main practical reason for records: without them you would need a separate parallel 1D array for each field (IDs, names, dates, marks, flags) and would have to keep the same index lined up across all of them.
bullets: DECLARE Class : ARRAY[1:30] OF StudentRecord creates 30 records.
Syntax order: ArrayName[Index].FieldName.
A FOR loop over the index processes every record; inside it, each field is used like a normal variable.
An array of records replaces several parallel arrays and keeps each item's data together.

examples.label: Saving to and reading from an array of records
examples.content:
DECLARE Class : ARRAY[1:4] OF StudentRecord
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER

// save: fill every record from input
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   INPUT Class[Index].StudentID
   INPUT Class[Index].Name
   INPUT Class[Index].DateOfBirth
   INPUT Class[Index].TestMark
   INPUT Class[Index].FeesPaid
NEXT Index

// read: average mark and names of students who still owe fees
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   Total ← Total + Class[Index].TestMark
   IF Class[Index].FeesPaid = FALSE
      THEN
         OUTPUT Class[Index].Name
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT "Average: ", Total / 4

examples.label: Trace with four records
examples.content:
Data stored:
Index | StudentID | Name  | DateOfBirth | TestMark | FeesPaid
1     | "S1042"   | Aisha | 14/03/2008  | 72       | TRUE
2     | "S1043"   | Ben   | 02/11/2007  | 58       | FALSE
3     | "S1044"   | Chen  | 21/06/2008  | 85       | TRUE
4     | "S1045"   | Dara  | 09/01/2008  | 41       | FALSE

Second loop:
Index | Class[Index].TestMark | Total | FeesPaid | OUTPUT
1     | 72                    | 72    | TRUE     |
2     | 58                    | 130   | FALSE    | Ben
3     | 85                    | 215   | TRUE     |
4     | 41                    | 256   | FALSE    | Dara
after loop                                       | Average: 64.0

256 / 4 = 64.0 (the result of '/' is REAL). Checked with an equivalent Python run.

sections.title: Justifying a record over separate variables or parallel arrays
content: When a question asks why a record is suitable, link the answer to the data. The fields all describe one entity (one student, one book, one parcel) and they have different data types, so no single array can hold them, but a record type can. Keeping them under one identifier means the program cannot accidentally pair the name of one student with the mark of another, which is a real risk with parallel arrays if one array is sorted and the others are not.

Records also make code shorter and clearer. A whole record can be passed to a procedure as one parameter, copied in one assignment, or swapped in one step during a sort, instead of handling five separate values. When the collection grows, an array of records scales with a single declaration, whereas separate variables would need new names for every extra item.

A record is not the right choice for everything. Many values of the same type that are processed together, such as 52 weekly rainfall readings, belong in an array. A record fits the attributes of one item; an array fits a list of similar items; an array of records fits a list of items that each have several attributes.
bullets: Purpose answer: groups related data of different types about one item under one identifier.
Benefit: fields stay together, so data for one item cannot become misaligned as it can across parallel arrays.
Benefit: one record can be passed, copied or swapped as a single unit.
Same-type lists belong in an array; mixed-type attributes of one item belong in a record.

rows: Counts, loop counters, array indexes, years
Signed number with a fractional part
Names, addresses, codes with leading zeros
Dates that are compared or subtracted
Many values of one type under one identifier
A list or table of similar values (10.2)
Data held in a file outside the program

All the attributes of one item under one identifier

diagram.title: From a real-world item to an array of records
nodes: Identify the item and list its attributes (ID, name, date of birth, mark, fees paid)
Pick and justify a data type for each attribute
Define the record type: TYPE StudentRecord … ENDTYPE
Declare a variable, or an array of records: DECLARE Class : ARRAY[1:30] OF StudentRecord
Save data to fields with dot notation: Class[i].Name ← "Ben"
Read fields in expressions, conditions and OUTPUT statements

analysisChains.title: Choosing types for a parcel-tracking record
steps: A courier stores, for each parcel, a tracking code such as "0093XK21", the weight in kg, the number of delivery attempts, the delivery date and whether a signature is needed
The tracking code has a leading zero and letters and is never used in arithmetic, so it is STRING
Weight can be 2.35 kg, so REAL; delivery attempts are counted, so INTEGER
The delivery date will be compared with today's date, so DATE; signature needed has two states, so BOOLEAN
analysisChains.evaluation: Five fields with four different types describe one parcel, so a record type ParcelRecord is the right structure, and an array of ParcelRecord holds the whole day's deliveries.

analysisChains.title: Record versus parallel arrays when sorting
steps: A program keeps student names in Names[1:30] and marks in Marks[1:30], matched by index
A bubble sort is written that swaps elements of Marks to put the marks in order
The programmer forgets to make the same swaps in Names, so Names[1] no longer belongs with Marks[1]
Rewriting the data as ARRAY[1:30] OF StudentRecord means each swap moves a whole record, name and mark together
analysisChains.evaluation: Parallel arrays rely on the programmer keeping every array in step; a record keeps each item's fields together automatically, which removes this class of error and shortens the swap code.

analysisChains.title: Spotting a wrong type from a failed calculation
steps: A variable AverageMark is declared INTEGER and assigned Total / Count
With Total = 131 and Count = 2, the true average is 65.5
The '/' operator gives a REAL result, which cannot be stored exactly in an INTEGER variable
Declaring AverageMark as REAL stores 65.5 correctly
analysisChains.evaluation: The type must match the values the program produces, not just the inputs: two INTEGER inputs can still give a REAL result.

examTips: For 'state and justify a data type', always give a reason about the data itself: whole number, fractional part, single character, two states, calendar date, or not used in arithmetic.
Write record definitions exactly in the Cambridge format: TYPE Name, one DECLARE Field : Type line per field, ENDTYPE; then a separate DECLARE for the variable.
Use dot notation every time a field is read or written; for an array of records put the index before the dot, Class[i].Name.
When asked for the purpose of a record, say it holds related data of different data types under one identifier, and tie it to the scenario's item.
Check literals in your pseudocode: REAL with a decimal point (5.0), CHAR in single quotes, STRING in double quotes, BOOLEAN without quotes.
commonMistakes: Declaring phone numbers, ISBNs or other numeric-looking codes as INTEGER, which loses leading zeros and cannot hold spaces or letters.
Declaring a result of '/' division, such as an average, as INTEGER.
Using CHAR for a value that can be more than one character, or putting a CHAR literal in double quotes.
Defining the record type but never declaring a variable of that type, then writing StudentRecord.Name as if the type held data.
Assigning a single value to a whole record (Student ← "Aisha") instead of to a named field.
Writing Class.Name[3] instead of Class[3].Name for a field of an element in an array of records.

quickRecall.question: List the eight pseudocode data types named in the syllabus.
quickRecall.answer: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE, ARRAY and FILE.

quickRecall.question: Why should a telephone number be stored as STRING?
quickRecall.answer: It may start with 0 or contain spaces or '+', and it is never used in arithmetic; an INTEGER would drop the leading zero and could not hold the other characters.

quickRecall.question: How is a REAL literal written in Cambridge pseudocode?
quickRecall.answer: With a decimal point and at least one digit on each side, for example 7.0 or 0.5.

quickRecall.question: What is the purpose of a record structure?
quickRecall.answer: To hold a set of related data items, which may be of different data types, under one identifier.

quickRecall.question: Why is a record called a user-defined or composite type?
quickRecall.answer: User-defined because the programmer declares its fields rather than the language supplying it; composite because it is built from other data types.

quickRecall.question: Write the statement that sets the mark of the second student in array Class to 64.
What does TYPE BookType … ENDTYPE create on its own?
quickRecall.answer: Only a definition of the layout; no storage exists until a variable such as DECLARE Book : BookType is declared.
